h1:
Things to Do in Phrae
Temples, old town and nature in one trip
intro: Phrae is a small town that's easy to explore on foot, and you can drive from one side of the city to the other in under ten minutes. But it packs a lot in: old, sacred temples, century-old pastel teak mansions, oddly shaped earth pillars you won't see elsewhere, and waterfalls in the green hills around town. We've picked the must-sees for every kind of traveller, with opening hours, entry fees and directions we've actually used so you won't get lost.

blocks.html: If you think of Phrae as just a stop on the way to Nan, you're missing out. This town rolls three trips into one: culture (old temples, teak mansions of the nobility), old town (Kad Kong Kao, the walking street) and nature (the earth pillars of Phae Mueang Phi, the Wiang Kosai waterfalls). The town centre is compact and you can walk between the sights inside the old quarter, while the nature spots sit just outside town. Rent one car or motorbike and you can cover the whole province. We've gathered all the must-sees below.

Phrae is an old Lanna town, so its temples mix authentic Lanna art with the Burmese style that the old teak traders brought in. Two temples you shouldn't miss are Phra That Cho Hae (outside town) and Wat Chom Sawan (in the old quarter) — different styles, but both excellent.

items.name: Wat Phra That Cho Hae (Royal Temple)
items.blurb: The guardian relic of Phrae: a golden chedi clad in tong jangko gold sheet, set on grounds of more than 175 rai. It's the year-of-birth relic for people born in the Year of the Tiger, and most visitors to Phrae come here first to pay respects for good fortune. It sits in Cho Hae sub-district, about 9 km from town.
items.meta: Cho Hae sub-district · ~9 km from town · Open all day, free

items.name: Wat Chom Sawan
items.blurb: The only Burmese Bagan-style temple in Phrae town, built in 1894 during the reign of King Rama V. The wooden hall has a beautiful tiered roof, and inside it keeps an ivory scripture and rare antiques. It's on Yantrakitkoson Road, only about 1 km from the city hall, an easy walk on from the old town.

items.name: Wat Pong Sunan
items.blurb: A temple in the old-town quarter right next to Vongburi House and Kad Kong Kao. Its highlights are a golden reclining Buddha and a glass viharn with a multi-spired chedi. Pay your respects here and you can carry straight on into the old town.

blocks.title: Tip for the spiritually inclined
blocks.html: If you want to do the full temple round, Phrae has a nine-temple merit route you can do in a single day. Most of the temples are inside the old quarter and within walking distance of each other, leaving only Phra That Cho Hae and the out-of-town temples that need a car. Go in the morning before the sun gets harsh and it's the most comfortable.

blocks.text: Century-old teak houses — the teak traders' legacy

blocks.html: There was an era when Phrae was a very wealthy teak-trading town. The old merchants and nobility built several large teak mansions, many of which still stand fully intact and open to visitors. This is a charm that's hard to find anywhere else.

items.name: Vongburi House
items.blurb: A pink pastel golden-teak house more than 100 years old, with gingerbread fretwork all over. Inside it displays antique objects and household items, and every corner photographs beautifully. It's in the old-town quarter right beside Kad Kong Kao.

items.name: Khum Chao Luang (Phrae Governor's Mansion)
items.blurb: A teak mansion in Thai-European gingerbread style with as many as 72 doors. It once served as a government office, with prisoners held beneath the raised floor, and today it's open as a museum telling the story of Phrae's rulers.

items.name: Ban Prathap Jai (House of a Hundred Pillars)
items.blurb: An all-teak house standing on more than 130 large teak posts, each around 300 years old. It was completed in 1976 and sits in Pa Maet sub-district, just outside town.

blocks.title: Approximate entry fees
blocks.html: Ban Prathap Jai is around 15 THB for Thais and 20 THB for foreigners, open daily 08:00–17:00. Vongburi House and Khum Chao Luang also charge entry fees in the low tens of baht. Prices can change, and it's worth carrying cash since several places don't take transfers.

blocks.text: Walking the old town — Kad Kong Kao

blocks.html: Phrae's old-town quarter on Kham Lue Road, near Vongburi House and Wat Pong Sunan, is still full of old wooden buildings kept in their original condition. It was the trading hub of the Phrae people from the reign of King Rama V onward, and every Saturday evening this street turns into Kad Kong Kao, the walking street where locals come to eat, shop and wander.

items: Kad Kong Kao (walking street) — open only on Saturday evenings, roughly 16:00–20:00. Expect local food, khanom jeen nam ngiao, souvenirs, craft stalls and the atmosphere of old wooden houses.
Cafes in old wooden houses — this quarter has several cafes converted from classic teak houses, where you can sip coffee and take in the old architecture all day, no need to wait for Saturday.
Photo walk through the old quarter — Vongburi House, Wat Pong Sunan and the wooden buildings around them are all within walking distance, easy to plan as a single loop.

blocks.html: Head just outside town and you'll find Phrae's natural side. The standout is Phae Mueang Phi, earth-pillar formations sculpted into strange shapes by wind and rain, plus the forested hills toward Wang Chin district with several beautiful tiered waterfalls.

items.name: Phae Mueang Phi Forest Park
items.blurb: Earth pillars and soil cliffs eroded by water and wind over ages into shapes like a town out of a fairy tale. You can walk the forest trails to see them, the scenery is unusual and great for photos. It's in Nam Cham sub-district, about 12 km from town.
items.meta: Nam Cham sub-district · ~12 km · Entry a few tens of baht

items.name: Mae Koeng Luang Waterfall (Wiang Kosai NP)
items.blurb: A multi-tiered waterfall in the rainforest of Wiang Kosai National Park, toward Wang Chin district. The water is clear and cool, perfect for escaping the heat for a swim, and pairs with the nearby Mae Koeng Noi Waterfall.
items.meta: Wang Chin district · Far from town, car needed

items.name: Doi Pha Klong National Park
items.blurb: Steep limestone mountains spanning several districts, with viewpoints and caves. It suits hikers and anyone after mountain views, and lies around the Long, Sung Men and Mueang districts.
items.meta: Long/Sung Men districts · Drive in to the spots

blocks.title: When to go for nature
blocks.html: Phae Mueang Phi is good year-round, but avoid the midday sun since it's out in the open — early morning or late afternoon has nicer light. The Wiang Kosai waterfalls have the most water in late rainy season and early winter; in the dry season the flow drops but you can still swim.

blocks.text: How to plan a trip that's worth it

blocks.html: If you only have one day, focus on the old quarter: walk the old town, Vongburi House, Khum Chao Luang and Wat Chom Sawan, then finish at Phra That Cho Hae. With two days, add Phae Mueang Phi and Ban Prathap Jai on the second day. The full nature route, like the Wiang Kosai waterfalls, suits anyone with a car and a flexible three days.

items.name: 1-day trip
items.blurb: Focus on the old quarter: walk the old town, visit the temples, finish at Phra That Cho Hae. Great for anyone stopping along the way.

items.name: 2 days, 1 night
items.blurb: Add Phae Mueang Phi and the teak houses, stay one night and walk Kad Kong Kao on Saturday.

faq.q: What are the must-see things to do in Phrae?
faq.a: Don't miss Wat Phra That Cho Hae (the town's guardian relic), Khum Chao Luang and Vongburi House (century-old teak houses), the Kad Kong Kao old town, the Burmese-style Wat Chom Sawan, and Phae Mueang Phi for nature. You get culture, old town and nature all in one province.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Phrae?
faq.a: One day is enough to walk the old quarter and visit Phra That Cho Hae. If you want to add Phae Mueang Phi and the teak houses outside town, plan for two days. The full nature route, like the Wiang Kosai waterfalls, suits a three-day trip with your own car.

faq.q: Is Phae Mueang Phi far from town, and what's the entry fee?
faq.a: It's in Nam Cham sub-district, about 12 km from Phrae town, roughly a 20-minute drive. Entry is a few tens of baht. We'd avoid the midday sun since it's out in the open.

faq.q: What's the difference between Ban Prathap Jai and Vongburi House?
faq.a: Ban Prathap Jai (House of a Hundred Pillars) is in Pa Maet sub-district outside town, known for its more than 130 large teak posts. It's open 08:00–17:00, with entry around 15 THB for Thais. Vongburi House is in the old-town quarter, a pink pastel teak house with century-old fretwork, and you can walk to it straight from Kad Kong Kao.

faq.q: Which day is Kad Kong Kao open when walking Phrae's old town?
faq.a: Kad Kong Kao is a walking street open only on Saturday evenings, roughly 16:00–20:00, on Kham Lue Road in the Vongburi House quarter. If you don't come on a Saturday you can still wander the old wooden houses and sit at the cafes in the area as usual.
